'''Brian Kidd Ridley''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (2 March 1931 – 22 May 2024) was a British [[solid-state physics|solid-state physicist]] specialising in [[semiconductor]] theory. He was an emeritus professor at the [[University of Essex]].<ref name="University of Essex">{{cite web | title=Emeritus Professors - School of Computer Science and Electronic Engineering | website=University of Essex | url=https://www1.essex.ac.uk/csee/staff/profile.aspx?ID=1517 | access-date=14 December 2017}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Ridley was born on 2 March 1931.<ref name="Who's Who">{{cite web |title=Ridley, Prof. Brian Kidd |url=https://www.ukwhoswho.com/display/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-32551 |website=Who's Who |access-date=2 September 2024}}</ref> He educated at the [[University of Durham]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Graduates |journal=Durham Colleges Gazette, 1950-1953 |volume=4 |issue=25 |page=3}}</ref> He received a BSc degree in physics in 1953 and completed his doctoral studies in 1957.<ref name="whoswho">{{Who's Who | title=Ridley, Brian Kidd | id=U32551 | volume = 2017 | edition = online | access-date=14 December 2017 }}</ref><ref name="newScientist1964">{{cite journal | title=New Scientist | date=7 May 1964 | volume=22| issue=390| issn=0262-4079|publisher=Reed Business Information | page=380}}</ref>

== Career ==
Ridley began his career as a research physicist in the solid-state physics division of the [[Mullard Research Laboratories]] in [[Redhill, Surrey]] (1956–1964).<ref name="whoswho" /><ref name="newScientist1964" /> In 1964, he joined the [[University of Essex]] as a lecturer in physics, later becoming a senior lecturer (1967), reader (1971) and finally professor of physics (1984), before retiring in 2008.<ref name="whoswho" /><ref name="University of Essex" /> He has held distinguished visiting professorial appointments at [[Cornell University]] (1967) and the [[Danish Technical University]] (1969), and has held research appointments at [[Princeton University|Princeton]], [[Stanford University|Stanford]], [[University of Lund|Lund]], [[University of California, Santa Barbara|Santa Barbara]], [[Oregon University|Oregon]], and [[Eindhoven University of Technology|Eindhoven]].<ref name="whoswho" /><ref name="frsCitation">{{cite web|url=https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28RefNo%3D%27EC%2F1994%2F32%27%29|title=EC/1994/32: Ridley, Brian Kidd|publisher=[[The Royal Society]]|access-date=13 December 2017|archive-date=21 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200621154651/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28RefNo%3D%27EC%2F1994%2F32%27%29|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Research ==
Ridley conducted work on [[negative differential resistance]] (NDR), [[instability|instabilities]] and [[Hot-carrier injection|hot-electron]] transport in [[semiconductor]]s. In the early 1960s,<ref name="newScientist1964" /> he jointly discovered the electron transfer mechanism ([[Ridley–Watkins–Hilsum theory|Ridley–Watkins–Hilsum effect]]) which underlies microwave generation in [[Gunn diode]]s, and he was the first to discover the [[impurity]] barrier mechanism for NDR, and to demonstrate its existence in [[germanium]]. He was also the first to describe the consequences of NDR instabilities in terms of propagating dipole domains and [[current filament]]s. The existence of these [[nonlinearity|nonlinear]] entities has been verified in a wide variety of solids. His work on [[Acousto-electric effect|acoustoelectric instabilities]] led to his invention of the microsonic analogue of the [[laser]]. He has made original contributions to the theory of [[Atomic electron transition|electron transitions]] in solids, particularly [[Phonon scattering|impurity scattering]] and multiphonon processes. This work is the subject of his monograph ''Quantum Processes in Semiconductors'', widely used as a reference text.<ref name="frsCitation" /><ref name="FRS" />

He wrote three popular books, ''Time, Space and Things'' (1976), which has been translated into multiple languages, ''The Physical Environment'' (1979) and '' On Science'' (2001).<ref name="whoswho" /><ref name="FRS" /><ref name="IOP Publishing 2000 pp. 55–62" />

== Death ==
Ridley died on 22 May 2024, at the age of 93.<ref name="Who's Who"/>

== Awards and honours ==
Ridley was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1994|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1994]].<ref name="FRS">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/brian-ridley-12177|title=Brian Ridley|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London}} One or more of the preceding sentences may incorporate text from the royalsociety.org website where "all text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License." {{Cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=16 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170710134855/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=10 July 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> In 2001, the [[Institute of Physics]] awarded him the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Dirac Medal]] in recognition of his four-decade long ''influence on the semiconductor theory''.<ref name="IoPDirac">{{cite web | last=Physics | first=Institute of | title=Dirac medal recipients | website=Institute of Physics - For physics • For physicists • For all | url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/dirac/medallists/page_38431.html | access-date=13 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="IOP Publishing 2000 pp. 55–62">{{cite journal | title=Institute Matters | journal=Physics World | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=13 | issue=12 | year=2000 | issn=0953-8585 | doi=10.1088/2058-7058/13/12/44 | pages=55–62| doi-access=free }}</ref>
